name: Cocoduro
tagline: German recipe and nutrition app that pairs creator meal plans with macro breakdowns and current supermarket prices.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The software here is not the hard part: a recipe store, a macro calculator and a shopping list generator are a well trodden weekend project. What you cannot one-shot is the content and the feeds behind it. Creator recipes are licensed work from named people, and a nutrition table that is actually correct per 100g across thousands of ingredients is somebody's ongoing data job. The price layer is worse, because grocery pricing is only useful if it is right this week, which means a scraper or data partnership you have to keep alive forever. Build the personal version if you want a recipe box that knows your macros, but expect to type your own prices and steal nothing.
coreLoopDIY: A local recipe box that computes per serving macros from an ingredient database, generates a shopping list for a week of chosen meals, and totals cost from prices you enter yourself.
requirements: internet access for Open Food Facts ingredient lookups
willingness to enter or import your own price list
whatYouLose: The curated creator recipe library, which is licensed content you cannot copy
Nutrition values someone else has already checked and normalised per ingredient
Price data that stays current without you touching it
A polished mobile experience with barcode scanning and offline use
Whatever gets added next month while your build sits frozen
moatNotes: Two separate moats stacked: recipes belong to the creators who made them, and grocery prices decay in days.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the thing people actually want is not a macro calculator, it is a decision already made for them: here is a meal you will like, here is what it does to your protein target, here is roughly what it costs at your shop this week. Every one of those three depends on someone maintaining content and data continuously. A self built version answers the calculator question and leaves the other two to you, which is exactly the chore the subscription removes.
notes: A personal recipe box with macros is a quiet afternoon; a live grocery price feed is a permanent job. The moat is licensed creator recipes plus supermarket pricing that goes stale the day you stop maintaining it.
prompt:
Build a local-first meal planning app for one person. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non negotiable:
- Next.js 15 with the App Router and TypeScript
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/meals.db, schema created on first run
- Tailwind for styling, no component library
- Runs with `npm run dev` on localhost only

Features in scope:
1. Ingredients table: name, unit (g, ml, piece), kcal, protein, carbs, fat per 100g or per piece, and an optional price per unit with a date. Full CRUD.
2. Ingredient lookup: a search box that queries the public Open Food Facts search API by name and prefills the macro fields from the result, editable before saving. Handle no result and offline gracefully, never block manual entry.
3. Recipes: title, servings, free text steps, and a list of ingredient lines with quantity. Compute and show kcal, protein, carbs and fat per serving, plus estimated cost per serving from the latest ingredient prices, with a clear "price stale" badge when the newest price is older than 30 days.
4. Week planner: a 7 day grid, each day gets up to 3 recipe slots. Show daily and weekly macro totals against editable daily targets stored in the DB.
5. Shopping list: aggregate the current week's recipe ingredients into one list, merged by ingredient and unit, with a running cost total and checkboxes whose state persists.
6. Price history: for each ingredient, keep every price entry with its date and show a small sparkline of the last 10 entries.
7. Import and export: a single JSON dump of the whole database, plus a CSV importer for ingredient prices so a shop receipt can be pasted in.

Out of scope, do not build: user auth, multi user support, scraping any retailer site, hosting, mobile app, barcode scanning, copying recipes from any commercial service.

Any API base URL goes in .env with a .env.example committed and .env gitignored. Seed the DB with 15 common ingredients and 3 sample recipes so the app is usable on first launch. Write a README with setup, the schema, and one paragraph stating plainly that prices are only as fresh as the last time the user entered them.
